Here is an excellent example of trading psych and stop loss management: The pair is EUR-JPY:

This trade could have gone one of three ways:

1. Winning trade (modest) 2. Break even (no loss, no significant gain) 3. Stopped out with a loss

I will post the charts in order first, then I will explain how to analyze (my opinion on how to analyze )

HTF:

Lower TF to show the FTR/FL/Kink

Close up view of the reaction:

Option 1: Wait for price to hit the MPL and short to the first modest target (target shown as dotted rectangle). This is straightforward, but would take discipline.

Option 2: Getting out with no loss/minimal profit: Clearly, we can see that this was not the best setup for a reaction. With that said, as soon as price engulfed the MPL...GET OUT! There is almost always a decent RT after an MPL is broken. This is out chance to bail without taking a loss. In some cases we can even come out ahead by a couple of pips. The key: knowing the exact moment when your trade plan is shot and having the discipline to shut it down.

My # 1 motto for trading: I focus on capital preservation.

Option 3: Taking a loss. If price was allowed to run, it would have eventually stopped out. As we can see, the bounce at this FL was weak. Try to avoid this..be an active trader who manages their open positions. It will cut down on the losses. Imagine if you could control a majority of your losing trades at BE? All you would need is a couple winners from time to time and your account would grow exponentially.

It is important to review every losing trade...we need to know why the trade didn't work out. That said, the more I trade, the more I am convinced there is far more value in being able to contain the losses as opposed to bashing my head against the wall trying to find out what I did wrong. Sometimes the market does something we weren't anticipating...that is OK. I'd rather become an expert of slipping out of a losing trade at BE

One Idea i am experimenting with (to get out of a losing trade without taking a loss), is scaling in to the position.

If I get in on a trade at the SR of a FL (where we tend to see a supply/demand reaction), I can execute a trade of "X" size. Assuming the MPL of this FL is still fresh (orders remaining in the extreme end of the FTR) I can add a second entry order in this area. The size trade I place in the MPL will be approximately 3X the size of the first entry.

Here is my reasoning: When the MPL is engulfed we tend to see a RT back in to the FL. Sometimes the RT is not deep enough to cover the initial SR trade (especially if the FL is wide). To mitigate for this problem, I place a 3X trade almost at the edge of the zone. There is very little draw down on this trade, and if price does engulf the MPL, all it has to do is RT far enough to bring the second trade to BE, then travel 1/3 of the distance towards the first entry before the entire cumulative trade is net zero or slightly positive.

This dramatically increases the odds that I get out of trouble since I don;t need as deep of a RT to cancel out my first entry.

On the upside, if the MPL holds, the R:R will be incredible.

Anyone think about doing it this way? Any drawbacks I might be overlooking

Here is a good example that just happened on EUR-GBP:

First chart shows the basics:

You can see where my first entry was (beginning of FL). I added a final position at the edge of the MPL approximately 4X the size of my initial entry. As soon as the FL broke to the downside, I was watching my net P&L calculator to wait for a deep enough RT back to the FL to cover all losses and spread/commission. As you can see, within a few mins there was a decent RT back to the FL. I was able to close the entire position for a slight profit (basically break even).

No loss incurred... of course I still had a protective emergency stop at approximately 1:1 RR on the inital entry in case price takes off and never comes back to RT.
